### Gentrification
Gentrification has intensified significantly since 1980, with rates accelerating sharply after 2000 [Source: ev-1].
The term was coined in 1963, but recent decades saw a surge as Americans opted for urban lifestyles [Source: ev-2].

Between the periods following the 2000 Census compared to the 1990s, nearly 20% of lower-income neighborhoods experienced gentrification, more than double the previous rate of 9% [Source: ev-2] [Source: ev-1].

### Inequality
Income inequality has widened substantially across major metropolitan areas since 1980. [Source: ev-1]
The U.S. [Source: ev-1]

Gini coefficient reached 0.40 by 2013, with metropolitan areas showing steeper increases than the national average; specifically, New York City’s Gini coefficient is 0.5469 compared to the national 0.40 [Source: ev-1].
Other cities exhibit extreme inequality patterns with Gini coefficients exceeding 0.54 and income ratios reaching 18:1 between top and bottom earners [Source: ev-1].
Atlanta (0.57) and Miami (0.57), along with New Orleans (0.56), also show high levels of disparity [Source: ev-1].

Multiple metrics confirm this widening gap:
*   **95/20 Income Ratio:** Atlanta and Washington D.C. [Source: ev-1]
stand at 18:1, meaning the 95th percentile earns 18 times more than the 20th percentile; Boston, New York, and San Francisco rank among the highest [Source: ev-1].
This ratio rose from a national average of 8.5 between 2007 and 2014 [Source: ev-1].

### Affordability
Urban areas have seen nominal income growth, but it has not kept pace with housing costs. [Source: ev-1]
Since 2000, home prices increased by 177% while median household income grew only 92% [Source: ev-1].
The Case-Shiller Index reached 325.78 in July 2024, representing a 225% increase since January 2000 [Source: ev-1].
This disparity is most acute in California, where price-to-income ratios range between 9.6 and 12.2, more than double the national average of 4.7 [Source: ev-1].

claims.text: The shift from manufacturing to service economies has further impacted affordability dynamics. [Source: ev-1]

Manufacturing jobs fell from 19.5 million in 1979 to under 11.5 million during the pandemic, while finance and professional services grew from 12 million to 32 million jobs, concentrating high-income professionals in urban cores [Source: ev-1].

Urban areas now have a higher concentration of educated residents (35% with bachelor's degrees or higher) compared to suburbs (31%) and rural areas (19%), driving up demand for housing in city centers [Source: ev-1].

### Displacement and Demographic Change
Gentrification is linked to demographic shifts and economic displacement. [Source: ev-1]

Gentrifying neighborhoods saw population increases and became whiter, with an average increase of 4.3 percentage points in the non-Hispanic white share and a decrease of 0.7 percentage points in poverty rates [Source: ev-2] [Source: ev-1].

claims.text: Displacement patterns vary by race. [Source: ev-1]

Residents from historically Black gentrifying neighborhoods tend to move to poorer non-gentrifying areas, whereas residents from other gentrifying neighborhoods often move to wealthier areas, indicating that minority communities face more challenges during these transitions [Source: ev-1].

Economic mobility has also declined; 48 of the 50 largest metros experienced worsening economic mobility for low-income families over a 15-year period, with only Houston showing improvement in income outcomes for those growing up in the 1990 versus 1980 (a 1.1% gain) [Source: ev-1].
